messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 41-year-old Vietnamese American dancer who came to treatment months after returning from relief work in a war zone, where he had volunteered with a civilian aid team delivering food and basic medical supplies. The event he returns to most often happened late in the afternoon, in that dimming hour when the heat had not yet lifted and the air inside a damaged school building felt close and stale. He had been helping move injured civilians into a corridor that had been judged safer than the street outside. There was burnt plastic and concrete dust in the air, and on one of the foreign contractors nearby he could smell alcohol, sharp and sour on the man’s breath, even in the chaos. When shelling resumed, people surged toward the narrow exit. Minh remembers a moment in which he pulled free from someone clutching at him and kept moving with the group. He survived, but another person behind him did not. What has stayed with him is not only the terror of that corridor but the conviction that, in the instant that mattered, he acted against the kind of man he believed himself to be.

Since coming home, the time of day has become charged for him. In the late afternoon, especially when rehearsal runs long and the studio light starts to change, he feels his body tighten before he can explain why. The smell of alcohol on a colleague after a night out, or a burnt odor from overheated stage equipment, can collapse the distance between then and now. He describes it as having no warning: one second he is marking choreography, the next he is back in that corridor with the same crush in his chest and the same certainty that something terrible is happening right now. These moments do not feel like remembering. They feel immediate, as if the room around him has been replaced. What follows just as quickly is shame. Even in the studio, with music playing and other dancers around him, he is overtaken by the sense that he is reliving the worst thing he has ever done.

Over time, Minh has come to believe that what happened revealed something unforgivable about him. He says he acted in a way that violated his values, and he cannot make room for the fact that he had been frightened and trapped; in his mind, that explanation sounds too much like excuse-making. He has also started reading his life since the war through the same lens. If a smell sends him reeling or the approach of late afternoon unsettles him, he takes that as proof that he is a lousy coper and that he cannot rely on himself. Because he doubts himself so completely, he scans his surroundings for signs that he might lose control again. He notices the faintest burnt smell before anyone else does. He checks who has been drinking. He watches the clock as daylight shifts, bracing for the hour he dreads. The more he does this, the more quickly those cues seize his attention and pull the memory forward in full force.

When the memory comes, it does not remain a picture of the past. It becomes evidence in a case he is constantly building against himself. In session he circles back to the same thought: if he can still be thrown back there without warning, if he still feels as though it is happening now, then maybe the event exposed the truth that he is weak and morally compromised. Each episode of reliving leaves him more ashamed, and that shame hardens his belief that he is not the person he thought he was. He has become certain that his reactions mean something damning about his character rather than something understandable about what he lived through.

This has begun to shape his work and home life. Minh still dances professionally, but he has started avoiding late rehearsals when he can, offering vague excuses to leave before the light changes. If someone in the company comes in smelling of alcohol, he keeps his distance and struggles to focus on partnering or timing. A burnt smell from lighting equipment has, more than once, made him step off the floor abruptly and lock himself in a bathroom until the sensation passes. He is embarrassed that his wife has noticed how the end of the day changes him; he becomes watchful and remote, as if preparing for something he cannot name. What finally brought him to seek help was the fear that this pattern was tightening around his whole life. He worries that he can no longer trust his own mind or reactions, and he hopes, cautiously, that if he speaks about the event directly, he might find a way to remember it without being pulled back into it and without feeling condemned by what he remembers.
